source: CARDI book "ដំណាំស្រូវនៅកម្ពុជា" (Rice Cultivation in Cambodia), by Men Sarom, Thuy Lina and Pheng Thimuny, published by CARDI, 2007, Chapter 9 (Harmful factors and management), sections 9.1.1 (Leaf diseases), 9.1.2.1 (Bakanae), and 9.1.3.2 (False smut). No elibrary URL visible.
text: This entry supplements several already-confirmed disease entries from earlier batches with additional causal-organism and fungicide detail found in this CARDI source, organized by disease: Rice blast (confirmed Batch 9) - causal fungus Pyricularia oryzae, spores about 18-24 x 8-10 micrometers, disease favored at 22-24 degrees C with 90-95% relative humidity, yield loss up to 20-25% under severe infection; the source names Pyroquilon and Tricyclazole as seed-treatment fungicides, and Benomyl or Probenazole as options effective when applied before symptoms appear and up to about 10 days after infection. Brown spot (confirmed Batch 9) - causal fungus Helminthosporium oryzae (also known as Bipolaris oryzae), conidia about 63-153 x 14-22 micrometers, favored at 21-36 degrees C, yield loss up to about 52% under severe infection; fungicide options named include captan, thiram, chitosan, carbendazim, and a Mancozeb+Triazole combination as seed treatment. Bacterial leaf blight (confirmed Batch 10) - causal bacterium Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae, cell size about 0.5-0.8 x 1.2-2.0 micrometers, favored at 25-34 degrees C; described in the source as having no fully reliable curative chemical treatment, with management instead centered on resistant varieties and clean seed/field sanitation, alongside a note that Pseudomonas fluorescens has shown some biological-control antagonism against this pathogen. Bacterial leaf streak (confirmed Batch 10) - causal bacterium Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzicola, cell size about 0.5-0.8 x 1.2-3.5 micrometers, favored at 25-30 degrees C with 50-51% relative humidity; the source names phenazine-5-oxide-based antibiotic treatments for chemical control. Bakanae (confirmed Batch 14) - causal fungus Fusarium oryzae (also referred to as Fusarium moniliforme), first reported in Japan in 1828 and now distributed worldwide, seed-borne; the source recommends seed treatment with fungicides named as mancozeb and benomyl. False smut (confirmed Batch 14) - causal fungus Ustilaginodea virens (Cooke), chlamydospores about 3-5 x 4-6 micrometers, seed-borne and first described by Cooke in 1878, later reported in the Philippines (1918) and Myanmar (1932); fungicide options named include Sulem (1:1000 dilution), Jinggamycin, Bordeaux mixture, Chlorothalonil, Metalaxyl combinations, Triadimefon, and Carbendazim.
caveat: This is a cross-source supplement, not a standalone new disease entry - each disease above already has a confirmed entry in the knowledge base from an earlier batch. Once repo access is available, the specific causal-organism measurements and fungicide names here should be merged into (or cross-referenced from) each disease's original file rather than kept as a separate file long-term. Fungicide/pesticide product names are recorded as they appear in the source for reference; farmers should still confirm current local availability, registration status, and application rates with an extension agent before use, since agrochemical product names and formulations can change over time.
